articles.title: Science news in review: Sept. 13
articles.description: Science news in review: Sept. 13 Welcome back to Hopkins, Blue Jays!While campus was quieter over the summer, there was plenty happening in the world of science. Here's this month's science news in review. Scientists locate a new target for cancer immunotherapy Recently, scientists at the Erasmus Medical Center found that cancer may interfere with the immune system before its defenders even reach a tumor. In a study published in Nature , researchers examined lymph nodes from patients with melanoma and found immune cells producing high levels of PLA2G2D , an enzyme that appears to limit the growth of cancer-fighting T cells. These lymph nodes are normally where T cells first prepare to respond to a tumor. Researchers used mice models to study PLA2G2D. They noticed that when PLA2G2D was blocked in mice, more tumor-specific T cells developed and tumor growth decreased. This approach was then combined with a treatment targeting PD-1 , another immune-system brake. This combination showed improved benefits in the study's models. Through this research, scientists have found a new direction for where to focus efforts in cancer treatment. However, further research is still needed to determine whether blocking PLA2G2D is safe and effective in patients. Venus's pale clouds may contain a much darker substance Through telescopes on Earth, Venus's clouds appear pale yellow. In ultraviolet light, however, they show dark patterns that scientists have observed for decades without knowing exactly what causes these patterns. In a study published in Astrobiology , researchers used observations and computer modeling to estimate how much light the material inside the cloud droplets must absorb to produce those patterns. Their results suggest that the liquid could appear surprisingly dark if it were collected and examined in a laboratory, even if the clouds look bright from a distance. This is because tiny droplets scatter sunlight, changing how the clouds appear. The study does not identify the mysterious light absorbing material. However, scientists now have a clearer idea of what measurements to test against possible ingredients in Venus's atmosphere. Satellites track ocean heat to improve hurricane forecasts In order to measure changes in ocean height, scientists at NASA are using satellites to study this year'sweather phenomenon El Niño , a climate pattern in which unusually warm water in the Pacific Ocean shifts weather patterns, such as storm activity. Essentially, the one of the satellites, Sentinel-6B , first begins sending data related to weather while flying shortly behind its predecessor, Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich . Together, they measure the ocean's surface with radar by recording changes in ocean height. These measurements matter because warmer water expands, so changes in sea level can help scientists estimate how much heat is stored beneath the surface. That heat can fuel a hurricane and affect how quickly it strengthens. Researchers plan to incorporate the newer satellite data into forecasting tools, which could eventually give coastal communities more useful warnings before a storm reaches land.

articles.title: Masked tectonic structures suggest Mercury contracted 40% more than its visible scars alone indicate
articles.description: The surface of Mercury is filled with craters, ridges and steep cliffs. Over billions of years, as the planet's interior cooled, the planet also shrank. Just as the skin of a drying fruit wrinkles when what is inside it shrinks, Mercury's rocky surface crumpled into ridges and cliffs as its interior cooled and the planet contracted. Mercury has quite literally grown smaller with age.

articles.title: AI automates 3D membrane mapping, matching manual results in a fraction of time
articles.description: Cell membranes and the proteins within them control many vital processes and play a key role in health and disease. But studying them in 3D images of cells has so far meant slow, manual work. A team from Helmholtz Munich, the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and the Biozentrum of the University of Basel has developed MemBrain v2, an AI tool that automates this task—cutting work that once took weeks down to a few hours. The study is published in Nature Methods.

articles.title: Physicists can’t agree on how the Universe works
articles.description: A massive worldwide survey of physicists has revealed surprisingly little agreement about some of the universe’s biggest mysteries. No majority backed the standard cosmological model, a leading explanation for dark matter, or any single theory of quantum gravity. One area of stronger agreement stood out: 68% said the Big Bang does not necessarily represent the beginning of time. Researchers say the divisions show just how alive and unsettled the frontiers of physics remain.

articles.title: Could the Clues to Ancient Alien Civilizations Be Hiding in a Bucket of Moon Dust?
articles.description: Most of our experience with the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) has been focused on capturing radio signals that alien species have sent out, whether intentionally or unintentionally. That creates a huge “synchronicity” problem - what if there aren’t any alien civilizations broadcasting radio signals now, but there were a billion years ago? The Milky Way is around 13 billion years old - hoping that we exist at the same time as an alien civilization that happens to be actively messaging is a huge leap of faith. But, according to a new paper available in pre-print on arXiv and submitted to the International Journal of Astrobiology by Lewis J Pinault, as associated researcher at the SETI Institute, and his co-authors, we could take a completely alternative approach to trying to find alien civilizations - by looking for evidence of them in lunar dirt.

These properties have attracted considerable interest in energy-saving technologies and thermal management.

articles.title: Southern Ocean may flip from carbon sink to carbon source under mitigation scenarios
articles.description: Plans to limit the global temperature rise to 1.5°C above preindustrial levels depend on reaching net-zero emissions and, in many cases, actively removing carbon dioxide (CO2) from the air. While this helps limit extreme weather, sea level rise, ecosystem loss and the risk of triggering irreversible climate tipping points, a new study, published in Science Advances, finds that reducing CO2 levels may have an unexpected effect. Climate simulations used in the study suggest that the Southern Ocean around Antarctica may switch from being an important carbon sink to being a prolific source of carbon.

articles.title: Tiny cyanobacteria may be the secret heroes of ocean carbon sequestration
articles.description: A process known as the biological carbon pump (BCP) moves organic carbon from near the ocean's surface to the ocean floor. That carbon often stays there for hundreds or thousands of years, making the BCP a primary source of carbon sequestration in the oceans. Scientists have thought that relatively large phytoplankton are more efficient at exporting carbon to the deep ocean than tiny cyanobacteria, but new research by Jingjing Zhang and colleagues published in AGU Advances now calls that belief into question.

articles.title: Why are the stars around our galaxy's black hole missing their companions?
articles.description: A new study suggests that the young stars orbiting the Milky Way's central black hole may have a surprisingly ordinary origin. But the black hole's influence may be what makes their origin look more exotic than it really is. Along with shaping their orbits, it may also destroy their stellar companions. The paper outlining this work was published in Astronomy & Astrophysics on Aug. 11.

articles.title: Earth From Orbit Is Unpredictable and Messy. Could 'Liquid' AI Clear the View?
articles.description: Monitoring Earth from above is a messy, inconsistent business. Clouds can block a satellite view, the angle of the Sun can create huge shadows, and orbital paths might not take a system across the same general area for weeks. That inconsistency is hard to deal with for traditional software, and can even confuse standard deep learning algorithms. But, according to a new review paper by researchers Raul-Alexandru Gorgan and Dorian Gorgan of the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, there’s a new type of frontier AI that could be able to help - bio-inspired Liquid Neural Networks.

articles.title: A New Design For A Plasma Engine Fuels On Only Thin Air
articles.description: Choosing what orbit to put a satellite in always comes with trade-offs. When it comes to Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO), between 100-450 km, there are distinct advantages. Remote sensing cameras can take better pictures, comms and radar require less power, and atmospheric drag will automatically clean up dead satellites. But there’s also a cost - air friction requires any satellite in this orbit to use an engine near constantly to stay in orbit, which in turn requires fuel - typically in the form of expensive gases like Xenon. So, as part of his PhD thesis at the University of Stuttgart, which is available in arXiv, Francesco Romano decided to solve that problem by using the very air molecules that cause that friction as fuel for a plasma engine to keep satellites aloft indefinitely in VLEO.
